Solid Energy New Zealand

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: I am pleased to take a brief call on the financial review
of Solid Energy. The way in which we defi ne and measure the success of companies
like Solid Energy goes to th e heart of how we run our economy. In the 2010-11
financial year, Solid Energy generated $828 m illion and recorded a net profit after tax
of $87.2 million. But that profit does not take acc ount of externalities. It does not take
account of the environmental costs of the company’s coalmining at Stockton, and the
acid mine-drainage into the Ng ākawau River and other waterways. It does not take
account of the increased greenhou se gas emissions from the company’s increase in coal
exports. Solid Energy is a creature of our tr aditional economic model and our system of
Government accounts, where we measure economic success by the financial bottom line
and the focus is on growing GDP.
That is what the Green Pa rty would like to change th rough Dr Kennedy Graham’s
Public Finance (Sustainable Development Indicators) Amendment Bill—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Where is he? Let him speak.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: He is in New York. That is why that bill is so important, because
we would be discussing different questions he re tonight in this financial review if we
had the 39 environmental indicators of prospe rity in our national set of accounts, and if
Solid Energy’s performance was evaluated in terms of those indicat ors. The profit line
for Solid Energy conceals th e death of hundreds of rare Powelliphanta augustus snails
frozen to death in the fridges of the Department of Conservation in Hokitika because
Solid Energy insisted on removing them from their natural habitat so that it could take
the top off Mount Augustus. Th e Green Party wants these exte rnalities to be taken into
account in both the company’s balance sheet and its annual report, and in our national
accounts.
One of the most serious extern alities, which cannot be adeq uately considered in this
financial review, is the impact of the comp any’s lignite mining in Southland. The large
profits that Solid Energy has made have allowed it to experiment with untried
technology. It is proposing to convert low-qualit y lignite into briquettes, into urea, and
into diesel.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: That’s just stupid.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: It is just stupid. Thank you, Mr Mallard. The Parliamentary
Commissioner for the Environment says th at the proposed lignite plant would be
responsible for the single biggest increa se in carbon emissions in New Zealand’s
history. The Government went to Rio, but it should not have  been proud to be at Rio,
because shareholding Ministers should have seen the irresponsibil ity in Solid Energy
being allowed to proceed with lignite mining in Southland.
In 2009 New Zealand in Copenhagen took responsibility for reducing our annual
greenhouse gas emissions to between 10 to  20 percent below 1990 levels by 2020, yet
26 Jun 2012 Crown Entities etc. Debate 3347
our greenhouse gas emissions are on trac k to be 30 percent above the 1990 level by
2020. Solid Energy is making a major contribution to that. It makes no sense for New
Zealanders to subsidise new investment in  the carbon-intensive technology that Solid
Energy is undertaking in Southland. It make s no sense to allocate free carbon credits
that will equate to billions of dollars of taxpayer subsidies to this company.
It made interesting read ing looking at the Commer ce Committee’s report and the
transcripts, because there is a whole issue, too, around lack of accountability and lack of
transparency. There was an issue that th e shareholding Minister s—the Minister of
Finance and the Minister for State Own ed Enterprises—should have pushed the
organisation on. It will certain ly get worse with the mixe d-ownership model, because
there is no ability for Ministers to seek information from the mixed-ownership model
companies and there is no ability for the Official Information Act to apply. Solid Energy
declined, despite questions from members of the select committee, to release the
business case for its Southland lignite conversion projects. It also declined to release the
results of its annual public opinion surveys, which it claims substantiate its view that the
majority of New Zealanders believe that our coal should be developed if our
environment is protected. There is no abilit y, with that business cas e not being released
and the public opinion surveys not being rel eased—not being able to see the questions
that Solid Energy is asking—to actually look properly at the operations of the company.
So there has been very limited accountability  and transparency in the way that Solid
Energy does its business. Thank you.
Report noted.
Auckland District Health Board

items.speaker: Dr JACKIE BLUE
items.text: I am delighted to speak in the Committee stage of
this debate on the Auckland District Health  Board. First, I would like to acknowledge
the Minister of Health, the Hon Tony Ryall, for his leader ship in the health sector,
which is now, happily, a very settled sector that is in stark contrast to what it was before
we took over. Back then it was a demoralised and disenchanted sector, where clinicians
were considered part of the problem, not the solution, where wome n with breast cancer
were shipped off for radiotherapy in Austra lia, and where tens of thousands of New
Zealanders had been culled from waiting lists.
I would like to focus on the 2010-11 financial review of the Auckland District Health
Board, which the Health Committee viewed in  conjunction with that of the Waitemat ā
District Health Board. The committee made th is decision in its timetable because both
district health boards had worked collabora tively for some years and were working
towards practical collaboration, and it seemed sensible to review both district health
boards together.
Both district health boards share a chair—that is, Dr Lester Levy, a M āori board
member—and integrated back-office functions . I would like to acknowledge Dr Levy
for his leadership, in particular with reference to the Waitemat ā District Health Board,
which was quite a troubled district health board prior to his taking the chair. Dr Levy
reported collaboration at every level, which the committee was very pleased to hear.
Waitematā had quite serious financial difficulties in the past, recording deficits in 3
out of the last 5 years, but the financial result in the year under review shows it recorded
a surplus. The committee felt that this was actually an outstanding, dramatic, and
astonishing turn-round, and I think that that is all down to Dr Levy’s leadership.
I will just make some general comments about  Auckland District Health Board. It is
responsible for 87 percent of the people in th e Auckland Council wards; it is the fourth-
largest of the 20 district health boards. It covers almost half a million people, which is
about 10 percent of New Zealand’s populat ion. As at June 2011 Auckland District
3348 Crown Entities etc. Debate 26 Jun 2012
Health Board received about $1.8 billion in  revenue and employed 10,000 staff, which
is the equivalent of nearly 7,500 full-time equi valents. It had a sma ll net surplus for the
year under review of $142,000, which is slightly up fr om the budgeting surplus of
To get some perspective around this district health board, I would just like to make
the comment that it is the largest traine r of doctors, with approximately 1,200 doctors,
and at any point 630 of them are at various st ages of training. It is  the largest clinical
research facility in New Zealand. It provide s local hospital and out patient services for
more than 400,000 people living in the Auckland C ity area. It provides tertiary services
for the northern region, and over 50 percent of services are provi ded to people outside
the district. There is a significant what we call inter-district flow.
It is a provider of many sp ecialist services such as orga n transplants—that is, heart,
lungs, and livers—acute massive pulmonary embolism treatment services, paediatric
intensive care, major head trauma following neurosurgery, high-risk obstetrics, and a
number of other tertiary services such as clinical genetics and paediatric oncology for
patients in the northern and midl and regions. It is a very busy  district hea lth board and
there are many layers and complexities in its operation.
The committee was very pleased to hear from Dr Levy that improving productivity
was a priority area for the Auckland District  Health Board, and th at it was focusing on
greater productivity done more efficiently with  lower costs, shorter hospital stays, and
more satisfied patients—and who could complain about that?
I would like to just talk about the health Minister’s introduction of health targets,
because that really has put the minds of district health boards on productivity. These
health targets are national performance measures specifically designed to improve
performance. They have been accepted wide ly through the sector. They have not been
seen as threatening by clinicians. They pr ovide a focus for action. They are published
quarterly, and they cover such matters as  emergency departments, elective surgery,
cancer treatment waiting times—particular ly radiotherapy—immunisation, helping
smokers to quit, diabetes, and cardiovascular services.
The health targets work as benchmarks for di strict health boards, and in reality are a
league table, but, as I said earlier, they are not seen as threatening. In fact, district health
boards have used them to benchmark each  other and to step up. Quite frankly,
Waitematā has turned from being one of the poor  performers to being one of the top
performers.
Report noted.
Career Services

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: Kia ora. T ēnā koutou, t ēnā tātou
te Whare e whakawhāiti nei i runga i tēnei kaupapa o te pō.
[Thank you. Greetings to you and us collectively, the House, compressed here in this
evening’s debate.]
I am absolutely delighted to take a cal l about Careers New Zealand, which was
Career Services, the Government agency responsible for leading the career development
of all New Zealanders. It is because I have absolute confid ence in the contribution that
Career Services makes to the overall educ ation landscape, and the powerful support it
provides to all New Zealanders—young people in particul ar, including M āori and
Pasifika—because we, of course, are very  committed to those young people leveraging
off their educational opportunities and being able to define the skills that are relevant to
the career pathways that they would like to be able to take.
So, notwithstanding the deep scepticism that is being expressed by the Opposition
members of this House, I think it is important  to appreciate that Careers New Zealand,
26 Jun 2012 Crown Entities etc. Debate 3349
Mana Rapuara Aotearoa, is very focused on how it will help all New Zealanders, how it
supports school career guidance officers, and how it works with industry training
organisations, local councils, iwi and hapū, and Pasifika organisations, in order that they
are able to assist young people to design career pathways for themselves.
There have been a number of recent achieveme nts that I am very proud to bring to
the attention of the Committee, and which will have been reported at the select
committee. In July last year a Career s Summit was held, for instance, with
representatives from the private and public se ctors, to ensure the careers system works
for both employers and indivi duals, and contributes to  economic growth in New
Zealand. A career system action plan wa s developed, focusing on education to
employment and effective careers informati on, because, of course, rather than just
talking about how young people can be engaged, Careers New Zealand actually
provides services that support them to be able to have a real and meaningful opportunity
to develop their lives. We believe in young people being se lf-determining rather than
being dependent, unlike the Opposition members of this House.
Capable Auckland is a Careers New Zealand - led Auckland network, because, as we
know, a very big proportion of the youth of New Zealand is in Auckland. It is a network
of career and education professionals and industry and business people. It is a key
project in the Auckland careers blueprint.

items.speaker: Career education benchmarks
items.text: Careers Ne w Zealand has developed innovative self-
evaluation tools for schools a nd tertiary organisations th at help young people to assess
what choices they should be making as  they navigate their way through our
qualifications framework. Canterbury recove ry: Careers New Zealand is supporting the
rebuild effort, with a particular focus on matching skills with the developing labour
market in Canterbury. Why is that important ? It is important because we need to be
boosting all levels of the employment opportunities of young people.
The Canterbury Careers website has been launched. It provides information on
available jobs in demand and the skills n eeded in Canterbury, with direct links to
Canterbury jobs advertised in a range of places. There are 16,000 National Certificate of
Educational Achievement (NCEA)  students in Canterbury w ho are encouraged to plan
for their future, which, of course, is a fillip for them, because we all know how
challenging the times have been in Canterbury, and the idea that they can also develop
and progress their careers is extremel y important. So, 16,000 NCEA students in
Canterbury have been assisted. Careers New Zealand ensures that this support is made
available in all sorts of media that young people plug into.
Can I also talk about how young M āori people are being assisted. Nearly 4,000
young M āori, their wh ānau, and other influences have been helped to identify what
skills pathway they could pursue. Te T ūkirunga, which is a wh ānau-focused, culture-
based careers guidance model, is a fl exible programme that allows young M āori to see
what choices they might have, and to  do it in partnership with their wh ānau. That is
similar to Te Kauhanganui, which the Oppos ition members may know is the Waikato
Tainui initiative that builds skills for those young people in alignment with Waikato
Tainui’s navigational approach. Similarly, Pasifika young people: instead of just talking
about it, this Government has gotten on a nd focused on how we can help those young
people to be successful.
Report noted.
New Zealand Qualifications Authority

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to take a call on
the New Zealand Qualifications Authority. Can I start by acknowledging the wonderful
Ministers who are respon sible for education, Minister He kia Parata and Minister Joyce.
3350 Crown Entities etc. Debate 26 Jun 2012
They are doing an outstanding job, so I am ve ry pleased to be chair of the Education
and Science Committee.
Can I just say there are three core goals for the New Zealand Qualifications
Authority in the future. The first one is to en sure that we have a cl earer system and that
we promote recognition of learner achievement, the second is to ensure that we have
increased confidence in the sy stem, and the third is to en sure that for our young people
we have more portable qualifications across the world.
Can I start by saying that we have to talk  about the base that we started from,
because we actually cannot talk about the fu ture for the New Zealand Qualifications
Authority unless we acknowledge the very diffi cult situation that we  inherited. We had
16 and 17-year-olds dropping out of school with fewer qualifications and lower literacy.
The number of degree-level graduates did not improve between 2000 and 2008, despite
huge funding increases. We had low completion rates for courses, we had no incentives
for tertiary institutions to improve th eir performance, and we had a bloated
qualifications register.
One of the core jobs of the New Zealand Qu alifications Authority in the future is
about reducing this number of  qualifications. In 2008 there were 6,000 qualifications in
New Zealand. For a country with a working-age population of 2.2 million people, that is
appalling. Under our Government there is a re view. Our goal is to ensure that by 2014
the number of qualifications is down to 1,200. To  give you an example, in the area of
hairdressing, for instance, there were 72 qualifications. We will be getting that down to
nine.
We spend $4.3 billion in tertiary education each year. If we are going to achieve the
kinds of results through the New Zealand Qu alifications Authorit y that we need to
achieve, we need to do a whole lot of ot her things. One of t hose other things is
improving the financial performance of universities. There are 12,000 more core tertiary
places funded under our Government. We are i nvesting more in engineering, science,
and research-led learning. We have a target of 55 percent of 25 to 34-yea r-olds with a
qualification of level 4 or above.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Another target! Another one! Have you told John about this
one?

items.speaker: NIKKI KAYE
items.text: The Opposition says: “Another target !”, but what we know is that
we are working from an appalling record  under the last Labour Government, and,
secondly, we also—and this was mentioned by the Minister of Education—have some
very disadvantaged people in our country. We have, unfortunately, some very difficult
issues around M āori and Pacific Island education. What we are interested in is actually
having accountability, and that is what targets are about. That is why we have them. We
are able to focus Crown entities and other entities such as the New Zealand

items.speaker: Qualifications Authority and actually say
items.text: “We want accountability; we want some
targets.” This is not about pouring more mone y into the system; this is about ensuring
there is clarity and there is a simpler system  for New Zealanders to  be able to go out
across the world with decent qualifications. That is what this entity is now tasked with,
unlike under the last Labour Government, wh ere there were low completion rates and
where we had 16 and 17-year-olds dropping out.
It is also about ensuring that we know, through scheme s like the Youth Guarantee,
that some people do not suit classrooms. Fo r those people we are investing more than
$100 million in the Youth Guarantee scheme. Can I say that we are only able to do this
with the support of Ministers like Hekia Pa rata and the Hon Steven Joyce, who have
fought very hard in the education budget to  increase our education budget every single
year—by $512 million over the next 4 years—and that is because of the Hon Hekia
26 Jun 2012 Crown Entities etc. Debate 3351
Parata. It is a tribute to this Government that  we are investing more than ever before in
the education portfolio.
What we can also see is that we need to have more confidence in our private training
establishments. That is why, over 4 years, there is $29.5 million to reward completion
and innovation. But it is also about acknowledgi ng that we are pouring more than many
other countries into our student loan and allo wances system, and that is way out of step
with many other nations. I think 41 percent or  42 percent of our total tertiary budget is
spent on student support. You compare that with  Australia at 31 percent. If we want to
get the kinds of outcomes we want for young Ne w Zealanders in the future we have to
shift funds into things like research and into  things like training, not just into student
support, and that has been a big focus for this Government.
Again, it is about incentives in the system. So if we look at what—
Report noted.
Children’s Commissioner

Families Commission

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I do want to talk about the Families Commission
because the Government has made some moves to collapse the Families Commission
and the Children’s Commission together. One would think that the Opposition might
have some concerns about that, but in fact what we are more concerned about is the lack
of independence being shown by the Familie s Commissioner, under this Government.
After that Families Commissioner was a ppointed by the Minister, Paula Bennett,
suddenly we had a Families Commissioner,  Mr Carl Davidson, who in one press
interview rendered the Families Commission abso lutely irrelevant by declaring that he
was going to revoke the Families Commission’ s position on extending paid parental
leave. This was from the Families Comm issioner—the man who is supposed to be
putting families at the heart of what he advoc ates for. When it came to being asked a
question about extending paid parental leave, on the back of a bill that had been drawn
out in my name to do exactly that, because the Government was not prepared to back
extending paid parental leave, suddenly we  had a Families Commissioner who baulked
at it also. He said, and I am  going to quote him: “I mean, w ouldn’t it be great if none of
us had to go to work and we could just stay at home and get paid for it.”
That was from the so-called independe nt Families Commissioner, under this
Government, who in one fell swoop I think offended pretty much every woman in the
country, who knows that staying at home and looking after children actually is work. He
pretty much managed to make his whole co mmission irrelevant to families, in one
statement, all because he is working for a Government that insists that the Families
Commissioner takes a position that they would want to favour. That is not the role that
we should have for the independent Familie s Commission. The role we should have is
that it should be a challengi ng role of the Government. It  should be a role where the
commissioner is prepared to stand up and fight for what families want and what families
need. If that commissioner or this Government  were in touch at all with the stress on
working families, then they would know that extending paid parental leave is indeed
something that would make a big difference to  family life. At the moment, families do
not get any financial support after their baby is 14 weeks old. That means that many
parents are going back to work for financial reasons before they really want to and
before their family is settled into the new routine.
3352 Crown Entities etc. Debate 26 Jun 2012
In 2007 the Families Commission actually did a very comprehensive evidence and
research-based report, led by Dr Rajen Prasad at the time, and it was called It’s about
time. In that research and evidence-based report they determined that in fact paid
parental leave should be extended to 12 months. Suddenly, in the year 2012, under this
Government, we have the Fam ilies Commissioner feeling that he needs to say that that
no longer is a priority for his commission.
But it is not the firs t time. He is not alone  in that, actually, be cause strangely enough
I had the opportunity to talk to the Child ren’s Commissioner, also appointed by the
Minister, Paula Bennett, recently. He is prev aricating, also, on the issue of extending
paid parental leave. I have to pose the que stion to this House. What is the common
denominator here? Both the Children’s Commissioner and the Families Commissioner
are supposed to be independent. Those two entities were designed and set up to be
independent, to actually push the boundaries within the Government, on behalf of
children and on behalf of families. Well, that now has to be the sole domain of the
Labour Party, because the Families Commissioner and the Children’s Commissioner are
not prepared to do it in the face of that Government. The Labour Opposition is prepared
to stand up for children and for families. We  are at least prepared to put families and
children at the centre of what we are pushing  for and we will continue to perform that
role, even if those commissioners will not, under the current direction of the
Government. That means that there will no longer be a Families Commissioner.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and
speak to this debate on Crown entities a nd State enterprises. As a Crown entity, the
Families Commission is about to undergo a tr ansformation. The reason why it will be
transformed is that this Government believes in better public services. In turbulent
times, this John Key - led Government is de termined to take tough but necessary steps
to manage our debt, build a competitive economy, and deliver on better Government
services. New Zealanders know this, and they know it because they have seen 600 more
front-line police, they have seen 2,000 more  nurses, and they have seen 12,000 more
tertiary education places.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. I know we have had
a pretty broad-ranging debate, but that just goes beyond the pale, I think.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I will just remind the member that we are
actually on the Families Commission, so come back to that.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Recognising this after th e election, our confidence and
supply agreement with United Future promised this positive change: “The Families
Commission will have two broad functions—the existing functions will be headed by a
single Commissioner, and new monitoring, eval uation and research functions to drive
quality services for families. In addition a Families Status Report will be developed to
measure how New Zealand families are gett ing on, and government will re-direct $4m
over four years to fund extra parenting programmes and relationship education in
secondary schools.”
So what does this mean? Well, we are restructuring the commission, and this will see
its core activities streamlined through a leaner, more focused structure. It will be headed
by a single commissioner, down from the orig inal seven. That is right: less bureaucracy
in one fell swoop. However, it will be governed  by a board that will include Professor
Sir Peter Gluckman, as well as persons from  the public sector and philanthropic and
business representatives. This is about credible community input into the direction of an
important entity.
The commission will also take a new role , providing for inde pendent monitoring—
that is right, independence—evaluation, and research to measure the effectiveness of
initiatives across the social sector. Fundi ng will be reduced from $32 million over 4
26 Jun 2012 Crown Entities etc. Debate 3353
years to $28 million. This will be done pr imarily by setting up the new Social Policy
Evaluation and Research Unit.
If we are going to make a difference in our communities for our families who are
struggling, we need to be able  to invest in interventions that we know will work. The
body of evidence will allow policy makers, se rvice providers, and anyone wanting to
invest in those social services to make mo re informed decisions. It is about having
evidence-based interventions  that produce better long-term outcomes—something the
Labour Government of the 2000s clearly did not achieve through the Families
Commission. It is about our families, it is about our communities, and ultimately it is
about the kids in our country.
So financially, what does it mean? Well, it means we are going to prioritise funds
into areas that actually matter to New Zealanders: $4 million into the parenting
programmes, relationship education, and youth mental health initiatives—programmes
that have actually made a difference to New Zealanders in need. I have talked about the
$14 million that will be assigned to the Social Policy Evaluation and Research Unit, and
it will also have $1.8 million to take over the responsibility for the longitudinal study
Growing Up in New Zealand.
In summary, then, the Families Commission will remain an autonomous Crown
entity.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Ha!

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: That is right, Mrs Moroney—an autonomous Crown
entity. This is significant change for the commission in terms of its structural
arrangements, its work programme, its cap ability requirements, and its size. The
commission will continue to work on issues that are important for families, just within a
leaner, more focused structure. There will be an inter-agency team from the Ministry of
Social Development, the State Services Commission, and the Families Commission that
will oversee this transition. These changes wi ll be due to be implemented by 1 January
2013. Finally, may I say that—
Report noted.
New Zealand Antarctic Institute

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak on
this part of this evening’s deliberation. I have got to say that most New Zealanders do
not know too much about what goes on down in the Antarctic, except that, as our
colleague across the floor said, it is cold. Y ou have got to believe  that. But there are
some really interesting things that I woul d like to draw to the community’s attention—
the wider New Zealand community, that is.
The New Zealand Antarctic Institute was established, I think, in about 1996, and its
purpose is to develop, manage, and protect New Zealand’s interests in the Antarctic, in
the Southern Ocean, and particularly in the Ross Sea region. It provides a lot of support
for scientific research and conservation ac tivities, and it has a job to raise public
awareness of the efforts it is making in that pa rt of the world. I have to say that I have
now been in this Parliament  for 7 years, and I have listened to Lou Sanson, the chief
executive officer, and, more recently, Rob Fenw ick, the chair of the Antarctic Institute,
and consistently, this pair perform at a ve ry, very high standard. They are very, very
good people. They are a credit to our count ry. They run their books well—unmodified
audit opinion—and they have very, very good information and control systems.
One of the big developments over the last year has been—and particularly supporting
our Government’s emphasis on environmen tal issues—the Government funding the
development and installation of three 330 kilowatt wind-powered turbines, which
actually deliver more power per turbine than  any other installati on on the planet. They
3354 Crown Entities etc. Debate 26 Jun 2012
are performing at 140 percent of what they were expected to deliver, so that is pretty
good. If we put in another four turbines, we will be able to support the Americans at
their base just along the way from us, at McMurdo. That  is hugely good for the planet.
You have no carbon emissions, etc., but, more important, you have no waste and no risk
of causing damage through some sort of oil leakage. I think the environmental
stewardship of this programme is particularly good.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Who made them? Who project-managed it?

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Nobody in your electorate, that is  for sure. I think there is an
international component that we also have  to keep in mind here, because we are
operating in the Antarctic in partnership with other countries. The institute helped
Malaysia to accede to the Antarctic Treaty in October of last year, and we had a very
big issue that the institute managed to cope with in respect of encouraging Korea to set
up its base very close to our own but also to  use Lyttelton as the key point of entry. One
of the issues was that we did not at that poin t have the right sort of  diesel fuel to run a
ship down into the Antarctic. That problem got solved, thanks to our institute. We have
also had a very good donation in the last y ear from the Norwegian Prime Minister, who
provided $900,000 to the Antarctic  Heritage Trust. All of these things are happening
because we are running a really good opera tion down in the Antarctic, and, again, I
congratulate the management and the staff of the institute.
Of course, the closest relationship we have down there on the ice is with the United
States Antarctic Program. Our people are wo rking very closely with the Americans on
logistical arrangements, and I want to thank th e Minister of Defence, who is sitting here
in the House tonight, for making available a 757 as part of our ove rall contribution to
joint logistics with the Americans. The Amer icans have had a bit of difficulty over the
last year because they lost an ice-breaker and an ice pier, and they have had to ship in a
floating pontoon system into the area. So working with them helps rationalise the
logistical arrangements for th e difficult job of getting peop le from Christchurch down
into the Antarctic.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: The Antarctic’s exciting. Don’t make it boring.

items.speaker: JOHN HAYES
items.text: Yes, and I can think of some l ovely people I would like to send
down to the Antarctic and leave there to pe rmanently freeze, to become exhibits for
future polar explorers. With those words,  I have nothing further to say and will end.
Thank you.
Report noted.
Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chair. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia
ora. I rise to take a call on the Energy Efficiency and Cons ervation Authority. I want to
talk about the good, the bad, and the ugly in th is Crown entity, but first I would like to
acknowledge former Green Party co-leader  Jeanette Fitzsimons. In 2000 it was
Jeanette’s Energy Efficiency and Conservati on Bill, a member’s bill, which passed into
law the first ever piece of legislation in our country’s history to  explicitly address
climate change. Although we are having huge debates across the country about
electricity production, what  we often forget is that the most effective way we could be
reducing the need for electricity production is  simply to use the electricity we have
already, just more efficiently. We would lik e to acknowledge all the hard work done by
those Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority officials.
I will begin with the good. It  is good to be working w ith the Government through a
memorandum of understanding on the Warm Up New Zealand: Heat Smart programme.
This $347 million budget has recently been extended, increasing the amount of homes
we are going to insulate to 230,000. This is actually massive. It is making a real
26 Jun 2012 Crown Entities etc. Debate 3355
difference to New Zealand families, a real difference to kids’ health, and a real
difference to the economy. I note that th e economic benefits have recently been
estimated at $1.2 billion. From those 150,000 homes  that have been done to date, if you
laid the batt end on end across the count ry it would stretch from Auckland to
Invercargill, back to Auckland, and then some . So it is a huge victory. It is good to be
working with the Government.
But now I guess it is important to touch on the bad in this Crown entity as well. In
Budget 2012 we saw two very important Budge t lines cut under the Energy Efficiency
and Conservation Authority. The first was th e biofuel subsidies. This Government
drastically changed the good mandate scheme  that the Labour Government formerly
had, and put in a woefully inadequate subsidy, in the Biodiesel Grants Scheme, of 50c.
It was absolutely inadequate. The take-up was pitifully poor, and now the Government
has scrapped it. We can only hope that the Government now returns to a mandatory
scheme, if it actually wants to see biofuels being used in New Z ealand. It is a huge
issue, because, look, we are importing $8 billion in oil from some pretty unsavoury
countries around the world. It is a huge stra tegic economic risk, but the Government is
not doing anything about it. It is scrapping the biofuel grant.  It is not doing enough to
promote electric vehicles. It is definitely  not doing enough for public transport. New
Zealand could actually be self-sustainable in liquid fuels and other transport fuels, using
sustainable biofuels from wood waste, other agricultura l by-products, electric vehicles,
and a greater investment in public transport.
The other bad in the Budget was the sc rapping of the solar hot-water grants
scheme—again, a scheme that was doing a pretty good job. We would have liked to
actually see it enhanced. We should have seen the scheme enhanced to include
photovoltaic solar panels. They have dropped about 50 percent in price in the last 18
months. We could be producing a huge amount of electricity from the energy wastage
just hitting our roofs, if the Government  support included maybe a grants scheme,
supported with low-interest lo ans, and maybe helped facili tate a council rates payback
scheme, which has worked pretty effectively in Nelson.
And then you have got the ugly. We have seen the good, we have seen the bad, and
now the ugly. The Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority is struggling, because
the Government’s entire focus when it come s to energy issues—and you just need to
look at the Energy Strategy—is to  “drill it, mine it, frack it” . It is the only plan the
Government has got. In fact, the Minister for Climate Change Issues last week, in
response to my questions, said deliberately he wants to stim ulate the risky, deep-sea oil
industry, despite what we know. There are going to be hardly any jobs for New
Zealanders, hardly any taxes, hardly any royalties, and the pr ofits are going to go
offshore. So instead of a Crown petrol eum and minerals agency, why does this
Government not consider a Crown renewa ble energy agency, maybe under the Energy
Efficiency and Conservation Agency—it is doing some pretty good work in
conservation. Why do we not have a Government  department that is actually focusing
on rolling out renewable energy? We could be building tens of thousands of green jobs.
We could actually be boosting the economy in  a sustainable fashion. We could actually
be leveraging our advantages. Just look at the Pure Advant age report about a $6 trillion
dollar industry.

items.speaker: Hon Chris Tremain
items.text: We’ve got the second-most amount of renewable energy levels
in the world.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Yep, we are getting there, but what we are seeing under this
Government is all the focus not on getting it to 90 percent—which is its target. It is
another one of the National Government’s target s, but it is one that  it is doing nothing
about achieving. Instead, it is  sitting on its hands, subs idising the oil industry,
3356 Crown Entities etc. Debate 26 Jun 2012
subsidising the carbon polluters—$1.5 billion in  the emissions trading scheme in the
last financial year. So we see this Gove rnment sitting on its hands, but actively
promoting risky deep-sea drill ing. The sad thing is we ar e missing that green race,
which Pure Advantage pointed to. We could be doing so much better—not only making
our kids healthier through a good insulation scheme but also providing prosperity and
lifting them out of poverty. Kia ora.
Report noted.
Commerce Commission

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: I am speaking on the Commerce
Commission vote, which is a very, very im portant vote and Crown entity, indeed. I do
note and acknowledge that the Commerce Committee may, in fact, have missed on page
5 of the report a slight mistake there.
The Commerce Commission plays an essential part in the monitoring and enforcing
of a very, very important part of the regul atory regime across Ne w Zealand. Part 4 of
the Commerce Act obviously gets a lot of attention in the way that it has played out in
courts, and merits reviews and inputs reviews, etc. I do note that, and the committee did
talk about that, plus some other matters, in its report.
One of the facets of New Zealand being a small economy is that in some instances
where there are one or two large players th ey can, potentially, exploit their dominant
position or monopoly-type position, or perhaps drive monopoly rents. Of course, that is
not acceptable to anyone at all—at least, I am sure, not to most members in this
Chamber.
One of the harder parts about the commission’s vote is that there is an estimate there
in its outputs and deliverables, but it is actually very hard to estimate the time frames
under which judicial processes do happen. So th at does create difficulties for that vote
and can provide, perhaps, uncertainty out ther e in the commercial space. It can allow so
much for judicial reviews, judi cial processes, or testing in court, and then a review can
happen, so these may well cross over into new financial years. There can be difficulties
there, but I do acknowledge that the commission is doing a very good job, and the
committee generally noted that in its report here before the Committee of the whole
House.
One point in the report that the committee noted is that it di d ask the commission
about issues around convergence, particularly  in and around broadcasting. I think that
was pretty wise of the committee, because of the challenges of all things governance. In
fact, as mentioned here in the report on the Commerce Commission, to put it in a simple
way, that bit of glass in our lounges that we all traditionally call the TV or the television
is actually only a bit of glass. Although we  all probably call it a TV, it can now receive
data or content traditionally by analog signa l, although that is switching off across the
country over the next 18 months; by digital—as  DTT, or digital terrestrial television—
by satellite; or by cable in some instances. In fact, many TVs now come with either a
Wi-Fi or an ethernet enabler. Additions can  be put on; other little modules can be put
on. The simple message there is the challenges for organisations and entities such as the
Commerce Commission in broa dcasting, you name it, having to deal with a rapidly
changing digital environment under which content can now be delivered by many
means that were not even contemplated when  much of the legislation—be it commerce-
type legislation or even broadcasting-type legislation—was put together, thought of, and
voted upon with, I am sure, the best of intentions around this House.
I do note again that the Commerce Committ ee talks about this on page 171, but I
make the point that we just ha ve to make sure that we maintain flexibility, and perhaps
be platform-neutral, as within this Parliame nt here we devise regulatory regimes and
26 Jun 2012 Crown Entities etc. Debate 3357
models that entities like the Commerce Co mmission look after. There is also the
example that a person can now read on a tablet or an iPad things off the internet, they
can listen to the radio, they can watch TV, or  they can watch a movie, and all of those
can be from either within New Zealand or af ar. They can be live, recorded, sped up, or
slowed down as the user wants.
My point is that with regard to much of the rules and regulations that entities like the
Commerce Commission have to look after, we may actually have to have a look at some
of these models, simply because technology and the real world, if you like, are moving
at such a fast pace that there are grey ar eas—which the committee did start to have a
look at here—of where governance  is black and white and wher e it is grey. Of course,
there are sovereignty issues around things  that ultra-fast broadband brings upon our
economy.
Report noted.
Retirement Commissioner

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I rise to take a call on th e financial review of the

superannuation and the issues th at face our country in terms of how we are going to be
able to afford superannuation for future gene rations. It is very di sappointing that we
have not been able to reach any sort of agreement on this issue.

26 Jun 2012 Obituaries 3271 
TUESDAY, 26 JUNE 2012

OBITUARIES 
Major Hone Hikitia Te Rangi Waititi QSO 
Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA (Labour—Ikaroa-Rāwhiti): I seek to move a non-
debatable motion relating to the passing of Major Hone Hikitia Te Rangi Waititi QSO, 
JP. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is none. 
Hon PAREKURA HOROMIA : Ka whakatau ahau , Kia arongia e te Whare t ēnei, 
arā,  kua rere atu a Hone Hikitia Te Rangi Waititi QSO, t ētahi o ng ā tino pakeke o 
tātou, te rangatira m ōrehu o Te R ōpū Māori e 28, ā, ngauhia ana ō tātou ngākau puta 
noa te motu e tēnei ngaronga, tangi ana hoki.  
[I move, That the House note that Hone Hikitia  Te Rangi Waititi QSO, one of our 
great elders, an esteemed survivor of the 28 th Māori Battalion, has pa ssed on, and that 
Māoridom throughout the nation feel this loss and grieve as well.] 
Major John Waititi was the last surv iving company commander of the 28 th Māori 
Battalion, in C Company. He fought in World War II, and wa s well respected and loved 
by his company. He was a humble man with str ong leadership characteristics. He went 
to Te Aute College from 1935 to 1938. While over in Italy he was wounded three times. 
From there, the company moved on to fight  in North Africa and Italy. Major Waititi 
said the comradeship of C Company was cem ented on the battlefield of about a dozen 
battlefields, from Olympus Pass to Cassino:  “You develop this closeness because you 
realise if it wasn’t for your mates, then you might have lost your own life. They were 
there to cover me. I covered them. These thin gs are set aside as being sacred to us, 
particularly those relating to the men who died.” 
Following Major Hone Waititi’s return to New Zealand, he was elected president of 
the Māori Battalion. He and his first wife, Ma taku Allison, farmed at Te Waiti. Much 
later in life he married his current wife , Judy Clifford-Waititi, and they have two 
children, Kahurangi and Haimoana. 
Major John Waititi looked after his men wh en they returned, creating employment 
opportunities and doing what he could to suppor t them to return to life back in New 
Zealand. I had the privilege of attending his 90 th birthday. He was a rare breed and a 
special man. He will be sorely missed by all M āoridom and New Zealanders generally. 
He has returned to his ancestral marae of  Kauaetangohia, in Ca pe Runaway, where he 
will lie in state until Thursday. 
Motion agreed to. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Better Public Services Targets—Announcement 
1. JOHN HAYES (National—Wairarapa) to the Minister of Finance: What steps 
is the Government taking to get better re sults and value for money from the public 
service? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : The Government is determined to 
continue to provide a high-leve l, if not better, Public Serv ice with less resource, so we 
have set ambitious targets across 10 resu lts, which were announced yesterday. The 
3272 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jun 2012 
targets focus on difficult issues like re ducing crime, reduci ng long-term welfare 
dependency, and reducing educational unde rachievement. Progress will be reported 
regularly as data becomes available, so New Zealanders can see how we are tracking.  
John Hayes: Why is getting better results important?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : As we have worked through, in tougher times, Government 
spending, it has become clear th at the previous Government liked to demonstrate that it 
cared by getting more money. We are going to  show that we care—and we are showing 
that we care—by getting actual results. We have been shifting the Public Service culture 
in this direction. Keeping one more teenager  on the rails is actually the lowest-cost 
result that we can get, so it is a better Public Service, and we save money.  
Hon David Parker : Does his target for benefit numbers mean that the number of 
people on working-age benefits in 2017, if he ac hieves his target, will be 20,000 higher 
than when he took office 9 years earlier, if New Zealand is unlucky enough to still have 
him in power? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: And it is only the residents of “Planet Labour” who overlook 
the fact that there was a global recession along the way.  
Hon David Parker : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Th e Minister did not 
address my question as to whether my figure was correct.  
Mr SPEAKER: Well, if the member wanted hi s question answered he should not 
have put the last bit on the question. I am afraid that he gave the Minister a let off the 
hook that way.  
John Hayes: How will the Government and the Public Service go about achieving 
better results?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH: In the first place, by focusing on making a difference, rather 
than just getting more money, which has been the culture up to 2009. Secondly, by 
working more closely together among depa rtments. But, thirdly, by looking around the 
wider community to see who can help us w ith getting higher levels of educational 
achievement or less offending in prison. Unde r the National-led Government the Public 
Service is not so arrogant that it believes everything has to be run by the Public Service.  
Rt Hon John Key : Has he seen any reports that  the Government’s attempt to 
quantify 14 different outcomes is “pretty mean ingless stuff”, and does he think it is 
pretty meaningless stuff to be tackling rheu matic fever, abuse of  children, and better 
education for New Zealanders—is that pretty meaningless stuff?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : I saw a report—well, I heard a report that I di d not initially 
believe, actually, because it was a quote from some chap called Chris Hipkins from the 
Labour Party, who said of these result area s—better educational achievement, less 
crime, and fewer vulnerable children—“It’s actually pretty meaningless stuff.” And on 
“Planet Labour”, I think it is.  
State-owned Energy Companies, Sales—Potential Legal Challenges and Directors’ 
Fees 
2. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
David Shearer : In light of his statements concerning litigation around the plan to 
sell off shares in Mighty River Power, is it the Government’s in tention to hold back 
some of the 49 percent of the Mighty River Power shares it is privatising to cover the 
risk to the Government of a successful challenge from T ūwharetoa; if so, what is that 
percentage ? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No. 
26 Jun 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3273 
David Shearer: Was the risk to the taxpayer of any litigation identified by the time 
of the Budget; if so, was it included as a specific fina ncial risk, quantified or 
unquantified? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : There is always litigation ri sk. That has always been known. 
The likely effect of that is not cost; the likely effect of that would be delay. 
David Shearer : Is it the Government’s intenti on that the taxpayer may need to, 
therefore, bear the risk of the T ūwharetoa or Māori Council challenge in court; if so, is 
this a deliberate protection of companies and individuals contemplating buying shares? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : We live in a democracy where people have the right to test 
their legal rights in court if they choose to do so. Whether someone would be successful 
in getting such an application heard in the courts, or successfully judged in the courts, is 
a completely different issue. 
Hon Trevor Mallard : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That was an interesting 
answer, but not one to the que stion that was asked. The question that was asked went to 
who was bearing the risk: whether it was th e taxpayer or the purch asers. That was not 
addressed. 
Mr SPEAKER: I will allow the Leader of the Opposition to repeat his question for 
avoidance of any doubt. 
David Shearer: Is it the Government’s intention that the taxpayer bear any risk of 
Tūwharetoa’s or the M āori Council’s challenge; if so, is this a deliberate protection of 
companies and private individuals contemplating buying shares in Mighty River Power? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: There would not be a financial risk; there could be a time risk. 
David Shearer: Did his Government encourage th e board of Mighty River Power to 
increase salaries before partial privatisa tion in order to avoid the embarrassment of 
salaries skyrocketing after the sale? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: No. I would note that in the 9 years that Labour was in office, 
the chief executive’s salary at Mighty River Power trebled. 
David Shearer: In light of his answer, did he th ink that was a good justification for 
the increase in salaries this time around with Mighty River Power? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Contrary to what the member might think, I have not been 
asked about salaries today; I was asked about directors’ fees. 
David Shearer : Has he seen the analysis by Ernst and Young that Mighty River 
Power, Genesis, and Meridian Energy are well  run by international standards, and is he, 
therefore, aware that any effort to extract further profits from these companies will be at 
the risk of either asset stripping or increasing power prices? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: If they want to increase power pr ices all they need to do is go 
and ask Labour, because Labour got them up by 72 percent. 
Dr Russel Norman: In his answer to th e earlier question, is the Prime Minister now 
admitting that the legal action, or potential legal action, from Tūwharetoa and the Māori 
Council could delay the asset sale programme? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: There is always that risk from litigation; that has been known 
for a very long period of time. I do not think it is necessarily likely. I am just saying that 
that is always a possibility. 
Dr Russel Norman : Given his reported statement that he is unconcerned and 
unsurprised that directors’ fees would doubl e if his asset sale policy goes ahead, why 
did he not tell New Zealanders earlier th at privatisation woul d mean that power 
company directors would see their pay double, paid for out of power bills? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I am not sure I have ever been asked that question, either. I 
was asked about an increase in the fees for the directors of Mighty River Power, not in 
the context of what percentage  they were moving. It is wo rth remembering that Mighty 
River Power is a company of revenue in the order of about $1.5 billion, so changes of 
3274 Questions for Oral Answer 26 Jun 2012 
the magnitude that has been outlined by the member are not likely to have any impact 
on power prices. 
Dr Russel Norman : Has the Prime Minister seen th e document from Treasury that 
indicates that director fees are likely to double, and where does he think these 
companies are going to get the money from, if not from consumers? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : No, I have not seen that repo rt. Secondly, I think it is very 
unlikely. History tells us that companies that  are run privately, wh ere they are listed on 
the stock exchange, have con tinuous disclosure, and are open  to all of the analysis by 
stockbrokers and by analysts in the market, tend to be better run. 
Better Public Services Targets—Reducing Long-term Welfare Dependence 
3. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister for Social Development : What 
commitments has the Government made to reduce long-term welfare dependency? 
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Minister for Social Development) : As part of this 
Government’s Better Public Services pr ogramme we have committed to reducing the 
number of long-term benefici aries. After legislation cha nges next year, this will 
combine those currently on the unemployment -related benefit, sickness benefit, DPB 
with children over 14 years, widows benef it, and women alone benefit. Jobseeker 
support is projected to have 130,000 people on it, 78,000 of whom will have been on a 
benefit for more than 12 months. We will reduce that by 30 percent. 
Melissa Lee: How does this target to reduce lo ng-term welfare dependency fit with 
the Government’s current welfare reforms? 
Hon PAULA BENNETT : This is part of our investment approach. Under the 
welfare reform programme, when you look at how we are going to work with people 
who are on benefits, the reality is that for those who are particularly on benefits long 
term and for longer than 12 months, I think they can expect to see more support going 
into them, more help for the training that they need to get them into work, and the 
upskilling to help them get those jobs that they desperately want and need. 
Jacinda Ardern : Does she consider her target to reduce the number of long-term 
beneficiaries by 30 percent by 2017 ambitious enough, when it means the number will 
still be 20,000 higher than when she took office? 
Hon PAULA BENNETT : That is not actually factually  correct, and I will take the 
member through as to why. 
Jacinda Ardern: Show me. 
Hon PAULA BENNETT : I can take the member through, actually, and I am quite 
happy to table this, if that would help. So, for an example, in March 2007, considering 
those who were on the unemployment benefit,  those who were on the sickness benefit, 
and those who were on the domestic purposes benefit with children aged 14-plus, we 
had 61,551; in March 2008—if that helps the member—we had 52,288. Look at the 
policy. If the member looks at the target , how we are making it up, and the reductions, 
20,000 is factually incorrect. 
Hon David Parker : I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I would take the Minister 
up on her offer to table that document. 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! If the Minister was quoting from an official document—
[Interruption] It is not an official document, so the member cannot— 
Hon David Parker : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Minister said during 
her answer to the question that she was willing to table the document. 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! It is absolute ly up to the Minister . Members cannot raise 
points of order about that matter. 
Hon David Parker : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Next time the Minister 
makes that statement, should I take a point of order that her statements are— 
26 Jun 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 3275 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! The House does not need to waste time like this. The 
member knows that if Ministers are quoting from official documents, the member can 
most certainly require to have them table d. We checked, and the Minister has advised 
that it is not an official departmental docum ent. It is presumably information prepared 
for her answer, and it is up to  her whether she seeks leave to  table it. We will see what 
happens shortly. 
Melissa Lee: How many people currently on benefits who have been on for longer 
than 12 months will be included as part of this target? 
Hon PAULA BENNETT : I think this might help with the previous question, as 
well. As at April 2012, 135,416 people were receiving benefits that will make up 
jobseeker support. Of this number, 78,074 had been receiving a benefit for more than 12 
months. This is made up of 38,927 who are receiving the sickness benefit, 23,031 who 
are receiving the unemployment benefit or unemployment training, 12,212 who are 
receiving the domestic purposes benefit—sole parent—and 3,904 who are receiving the 
widows benefit. That is how that benefit is  made up. Those are the ones who have been 
on benefits for longer than 12 months. Those are the ones that we will be reducing. 
Hon Paula Bennett: I seek leave, as I think we s hould do at the end of our question, 
not the middle of it— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Order! The Minister will just seek leave.  
Hon PAULA BENNETT: I seek leave to table a document that was made up by my 
office, but which does give the numbers of those who have been on long-term benefits 
from March 1997 to March 2012. 
Mr SPEAKER : Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection? 
There is no objection.  
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House. 
Economy—Targets 
4. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance: Does he stand by 
his statement that “We are a government that thinks getting results is what’s really 
important”? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : Yes, particularly when you look at 
the progress we have made. We inherited an  economy that had been  in recession for a 
year, forecasts of never-endi ng deficits, ever-rising G overnment debt, record net 
international liabilities approaching 85 percent, and a near-record current account deficit 
of 8 percent of GDP. Despite many difficulties since, all of these have improved.  
Hon David Parker : As part of the Better Public  Services targets he announced 
yesterday, did he give Treasur y targets and milestones for wage growth, overseas debt 
reduction, or export growth? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Measures of those are made  every day. The accountability 
for economic management is crystal clear and occurs every time new data becomes 
available. The member knows that, because he comments on it regularly.  
Hon David Parker: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My question was whether 
he had given Treasury targets, not what the historical figures are.  
Mr SPEAKER: The member’s point is absolutely correct. He asked a dead straight 
question. He asked whether or not Treasury had been given targets for those matters.  
Hon BILL ENGLISH: No.  
Hon David Parker : As part of the Better Public  Services targets he announced 
yesterday, did he give Treasury target s for making New Zealand superannuation

CHARLES CHAUVEL (Labour): I think it probably is a sensible decision to take 
the Prisoners’ and Victims’  Claims (2012 Expiry and Application Dates) Amendment 
Bill as one question in the Committee. It is a short bill. I want to say just a few words so 
that those listening and members who have not had the benefit of sitting on the Justice 
and Electoral Committee do understand the context of the legislation. 
Back in 2005 Parliament enac ted the Prisoners’ and Victims’ Claims Act. This was 
in response to widespread concerns about  the decision of the High Court in a case 
referred to, and reported as, Taunoa, where an inmate sued the Crown because he had 
suffered what the court decided was an abuse not only of hi s physical well-being but of 
his human rights through the application of  what was known at the time as the BMR—
the behaviour management, or behaviour modification, regime operated by the 
Department of Corrections. What happened is that the High Court said on that occasion 
that the inmate was entitled to a substantial award of damages to, in part, indicate that 
the behaviour of the prison officers concerned—sanctioned, it seemed, by the 
department—was not condoned by the court. Th ere was real concern at the time about 
the position of those who had suffered loss— physical or otherwise—as a result of the 
misdeeds of offenders who were serving time in prison and had received a windfall 
payment of compensation through the application of the precedent in Taunoa. As a 
result of that concern, the 2005 legislation was enacted. 
The 2005 legislation, as can be seen on its face, was always intended to be temporary 
in effect. There are two sunset clauses in th at Act. Part 1 of the bill before us in 
26 Jun 2012 Prisoners’ & Victims’ Claims (Expiry etc.) Amdt Bill 3313 
Committee today would extend on e of the sunset clauses, and Part 2 would extend the 
other, for a period of 1 year. The reason for this extension was canvassed in the second 
reading debate. There was, as is known, a ch ange of Minister of  Justice between the 
previous election and now. Fo r whatever reason, the Order Paper was not in sufficient 
order to see the legislati on that was proposed to repl ace the 2005 Act brought through 
all of its stages in order to be enacted. When that became obvious the Minister of Justice 
approached, as I understand it, a number of parties and said, well, what do you want to 
do with this legislation? Do you want it to e xpire, in which case there is a real risk of 
that; do you want it rushed through the House; or  is there some other way that we could 
deal with it—for example, by a short exte nsion of the current provisions of the 
legislation? My colleagues and I discussed th e issue. We could not see that it would be 
just, as far as the victims of offending we re concerned, to simply allow the existing 
regime to lapse. Although we would have preferred a considered discussion of what 
ought, if anything, to replace the 2005 legislatio n, we were in the end agreeable to a 
short extension of its terms in  order to allow that careful consideration of replacement 
legislation to occur. 
So that is the simple background to the bi ll that we are cons idering, with its two 
extensions of the relevant sunset clauses for 1 year only, to 1 July 2013. As to what 
might happen after 1 July 2012, it is my hope th at we will get some sensible discussion, 
both at the Justice and Electoral Committee and also, hopefully, between spokespeople, 
about what ought to be the replacement model for the 2005 legislation. In respect of that 
discussion, it seems to me that we need some information to be put on the table. 
First of all, how much use ha s been made of the existing le gislation? To what extent 
have the victims of offending found it a useful tool to try to make themselves whole as a 
result of having suffered loss through the wrongdoing of people who then ended up in 
jail, have themselves won damages, and then have had some of those damages go to 
their victims? The figures, I have to say, are a bit disappointing. Although the Minister 
was not initially willing to disclose them, she made some disclosures in her second 
reading speech, and further disclosures were  made during the estimates process by the

to say that this legislation wa s not the right thing to do at the time, but that is not the 
question before the Committee and perhaps later,  at the third reading stage, the House; 
the question is what we ought to do now with this legislation. 
My colleague Phil Goff made, I think, a compelling point in the second reading 
debate, and that is if we are going to rethink this from the perspective of the victims of 
offending, without violating the human rights record of our country  or the rights of 
those who are serving sentences in our prisons , how best should we do it? Well, first of 
all, what logic is there in  restricting any ongoing legisla tion simply to those who are 
sentenced to a custodial sentence? What  about community-based sentences? Why 
should people who have simply managed to a void jail avoid having to make some sort 
of payment to their victims in the event th at they receive a windfall payment at some 
point during their sentence? That just does not seem to be logical. Secondly, why should 
the windfall payments be restricted to paym ents from the Crown to the offender? What 
about if the offender somehow gets some e normous payment from a will, or from a 
Lotto win, or from some other means? Why should the victim of their offending have to 
go through the ordinary processes of suing in the court, all the expense, all the trauma, 
all the delays that we  know are inherent in civil litigation, in or der to try to recover

processing and the marketing arms of the company, and the fiduciary duties of the 
directors, so that the cooperative members receive the best possible price for the milk 
they, their cows, and nature produce. That ha s certainly been refl ected in the higher

Providing for Trading Among Farmers cuts acr oss this. It creates a significant risk 
for the future of New Zealand’s dairy farm ers and for Fonterra, because when a dairy 
farmer sells her units into the Trading Among Farmers fund she is selling her rights to 
the dividend, and also the equity in the cooperative. While the farmer will certainly 
retain the mutual supply and collection contract with the company, and voting rights, he 
or she is giving up the stake that those shares  represent in the financial ownership of the 
milk tankers, the milk processing plant, and other cooperative plant. That is where the 
risk lies.  
It risks introducing a tension between wh at the Hon Shane Jones has called the 
producer capital and the investor capital— those external investors who own the 
dividends from these unit shares—and, as the independent adviser to the Primary 
Production Committee, James Morrison, noted  in his report, those tensions will 
inevitably arise between the farmer suppliers to Fonterra, the external investors, and the

to be ongoing conflict between investors and the supplying farmers over the company’s 
strategy and the company’s opera tional decisions, and there is a risk that over several 
decades the ownership of Font erra and its key strategic decisions become increasingly 
separate from dairy farming.

base to use as a buffer against redemption risk, but submitters who oppose it said that

framed it as a choice between keeping Font erra New Zealand - owned or making it a 
target for large-scale investors who would be  more interested in the dividend returns 
from their shares. That is the risk—that this is the top of a slippery slope, which will 
lead to more corporate investment and ove rseas investment, which would weaken the 
voice and potentially overwhelm the farmer milk producers. That is why the Green 
Party opposes this bill.
